## INSURING AGREEMENT-COLLISION COVERAGE

If you pay the premium for this coverage, we will pay for sudden, direct and accidental loss to a:

- 1 . covered auto , including an attached trailer ; or
2. non-owned auto ;

and its custom parts or equipment , resulting from collision .

In addition, we will pay the reasonable cost to replace any child safety seat damaged in an accident to which this coverage applies.

## INSURING AGREEMENT-COMPREHENSIVE COVERAGE

If you pay the premium for this coverage, we will pay for sudden, direct and accidental loss to a:

- 1 . covered auto , including an attached trailer ; or
2. non-owned auto ;

and its custom parts or equipment , that is not caused by collision .

## A loss not caused by collision includes:

- 1 . contact with an animal (including a bird);
2. explosion or earthquake;
3. fire;
4. malicious mischief or vandalism;
5. missiles or falling objects;
6. riot or civil commotion;
- 7 . theft or larceny;
8. windstorm, hail, water or flood; or
9. breakage of glass not caused by collision .

## In addition, we will pay for:

- 1 . reasonable transportation expenses incurred by you if a covered auto is stolen; and
2. loss of use damages that you are legally liable to pay if a non-owned auto is stolen. A combined maximum of $900, not exceeding $30 per day, will apply to these additional benefits. The additional benefit for transportation expenses will not apply if you purchased Rental Reimbursement Coverage for the stolen covered auto .

Coverage for transportation expenses and loss of use damages begins 48 hours after you report the theft to us and ends the earliest of:

- 1 . when the auto has been recovered and returned to you or its owner;
2. when the auto has been recovered and repaired;
3. when the auto has been replaced;
4. 72 hours after we make an offer to settle the loss if the auto is deemed by us to be a total loss; or

5. if the loss is theft of a rented non-owned auto , 30 days after loss of use begins on the loss.

We must receive written proof of transportation expenses and loss of use damages.

## INSURING AGREEMENT-ADDITIONAL CUSTOM PARTS OR EQUIPMENT COVERAGE

We will pay for sudden, direct and accidental loss to custom parts or equipment on a covered auto for which this coverage has been purchased. This coverage applies only if you have purchased both Comprehensive Coverage and Collision Coverage for that covered auto and the loss is covered under one of those coverages. This coverage applies in addition to any coverage automatically provided for custom parts or equipment under Comprehensive Coverage or Collision Coverage.

## INSURING AGREEMENT-RENTAL REIMBURSEMENT COVERAGE

We will reimburse rental charges incurred when you rent an auto from a rental agency or auto repair shop due to a loss to a covered auto for which Rental Reimbursement Coverage has been purchased. This coverage applies only if you have purchased both Comprehensive Coverage and Collision Coverage for that covered auto and the loss is covered under one of those coverages.

Additional fees or charges for insurance, damage waivers, optional equipment, fuel, or accessories are not covered.

This coverage is limited to the each day limit shown on the declarations page for a maximum of 30 days.

If  Rental Reimbursement Coverage applies, no other coverage under this policy for rental expenses will apply .

## Rental charges will be reimbursed beginning:

- 1 . when the covered auto cannot be driven due to a loss; or
2. if the covered auto can be driven, when you deliver the covered auto to an auto repair shop or one of our Service Centers for repairs due to the loss; and ending the earliest of:

You must provide us written proof of your rental charges to be reimbursed.

## OTHER SOURCES OF RECOVERY

If other sources of recovery also cover the loss, we will pay only our share of the loss. Our share is the proportion that our limit of liability bears to the total of all applicable

limits. However, any insurance we provide for a non-owned auto , or trailer not shown on the declarations page , will be excess over any other collectible source of recovery including, but not limited to:

- 1 . any coverage provided by the owner of the non-owned auto or trailer ;
2. any other applicable physical damage insurance; and
3. any other source of recovery applicable to the loss.

## APPRAISAL

If we cannot agree with you on the amount of a loss, then we or you may demand an appraisal of the loss. Within 30 days of any demand for an appraisal, each party shall appoint a competent appraiser and shall notify the other party of that appraiser's identity . The appraisers will determine the amount of loss. If they fail to agree, the disagreement will be submitted to a qualified umpire chosen by the appraisers. If the two appraisers are unable to agree upon an umpire within 15 days, we or you may request that a judge of a court of record, in the county where you reside, select an umpire. The appraisers and umpire will determine the amount of loss. The amount of loss agreed to by both appraisers, or by one appraiser and the umpire, will be binding. You will pay your appraiser's fees and expenses. We will pay our appraiser's fees and expenses. All other expenses of the appraisal, including payment of the umpire if one is selected, will be shared equally between us and you .   Neither we nor you waive any rights under this policy by agreeing to an appraisal.

It is essential for policyholders to understand the limitations and conditions of this coverage, as it may not extend to all types of losses or all vehicles used. 13|Ride-Sharing Exclusions and Roadside Assistance Framework|"# Ride-Sharing Exclusions and Roadside Assistance Framework

The community centers on the interplay between ride-sharing activities, insurance exclusions, and roadside assistance coverage under a vehicle insurance policy. Key entities include RIDE-SHARING ACTIVITY, EXCLUSIONS, PART V, and AUTHORIZED SERVICE REPRESENTATIVE, which are interconnected through defined policy rules. Ride-sharing is broadly excluded from coverage unless conducted as a shared-expense car pool, while roadside assistance is governed by strict conditions tied to covered emergencies and authorized providers. The policy structure reflects a clear distinction between commercial use and non-commercial cost-sharing, with significant implications for liability, coverage eligibility, and risk management.

## Ride-sharing activities are generally excluded from insurance coverage

RIDE-SHARING ACTIVITY, defined as the use of a vehicle for compensated transportation through a Transportation Network Company (TNC), is explicitly excluded from coverage under the insurance policy. This exclusion applies regardless of whether the vehicle is personal or covered, and spans all phases of the activity—from logging in to the TNC platform to completing a ride. The exclusion is broad and applies uniformly to both intermittent and primary income-based ride-sharing, ensuring that no claims arising from accidents or damages during such activities are covered. This exclusion is reinforced by multiple relationships, including direct links to the EXCLUSIONS category and Part I liability coverage, which also excludes ride-sharing-related incidents [Data: Entities (31, 30); Relationships (137, 66, 56, +more)]. The policy clearly distinguishes ride-sharing from personal, non-commercial use, emphasizing that any form of compensation or profit-driven service disqualifies the activity from coverage.

## Shared-expense car pools are a key exception to ride-sharing exclusions

The SHARED-EXPENSE CAR POOL is explicitly recognized as an exception to the general exclusion of ride-sharing activities. Unlike compensated ride-sharing, this arrangement involves participants sharing travel expenses such as fuel, maintenance, and tolls, with no individual receiving a financial gain beyond reimbursement of actual costs. The policy permits this model because its primary purpose is cost-sharing rather than profit generation, distinguishing it from commercial ride-hailing services. This exception is formally acknowledged in the policy’s exclusions section, which explicitly states that shared-expense car pools are not subject to the ride-sharing exclusion [Data: Entities (97); Relationships (138, 115, +more)]. The distinction underscores the policy’s intent to support sustainable, non-commercial transportation alternatives while maintaining risk control. As such, individuals participating in such car pools may retain coverage under the policy, provided the arrangement adheres to the cost-sharing principle and lacks a profit motive.

## Roadside assistance is governed by strict conditions and authorized providers

Roadside assistance coverage is provided under Part V of the policy and is contingent on specific conditions. A covered disabled auto must be disabled due to a covered emergency—such as mechanical breakdown, battery failure, flat tire, or entrapment in snow or mud within 100 feet of a road—and must be towed to the nearest qualified repair facility. Labor on the vehicle is limited to 60 minutes per incident and must be directly related to the disablement. The insurer mandates the use of AUTHORIZED SERVICE REPRESENTATIVES, who are vetted and contracted to deliver services such as towing, jump-starts, lockout assistance, and fuel delivery. All costs associated with these services are fully covered under the policy when performed by an authorized provider [Data: Entities (203, 211, 212, 221, 222); Relationships (301, 320, 321, 322, 316, +more)]. Unauthorized service providers may be reimbursed only if their charges are deemed reasonable by the insurer, creating a financial risk for policyholders who use non-approved services. This structure ensures service quality, cost control, and policy compliance.

## Criminal acts and traffic violations are treated differently under policy exclusions

The policy distinguishes between criminal acts and traffic violations, with significant implications for coverage. CRIMINAL ACT OR OMISSION is excluded from coverage only if the individual is convicted or pleads guilty, and applies to the insured, their relatives, rated residents, or owners of non-owned vehicles. This exclusion does not extend to traffic violations, which are explicitly excluded from the definition of criminal acts and therefore do not trigger the exclusion clause [Data: Entities (56, 57); Relationships (115, 103, +more)]. This distinction allows for the possibility of coverage in cases involving minor infractions, such as speeding or running a red light, while still protecting the insurer from liability for intentional wrongdoing. The policy’s careful delineation ensures that coverage is not denied for minor regulatory breaches, preserving the policy’s utility for everyday driving incidents while maintaining integrity in cases of serious misconduct.

## Racing, stunting, and nuclear-related incidents are excluded from coverage

The policy explicitly excludes coverage for injuries or damages arising from racing, stunting, or nuclear incidents. Activities conducted on permanent or temporary racetracks, including pre-arranged racing or stunting events, are excluded under both Part I and the EXCLUSIONS section. Similarly, injuries caused by nuclear reactions or radiation are excluded, with a specific clause stating that if a vehicle is insured under a NUCLEAR ENERGY LIABILITY INSURANCE CONTRACT, coverage under the vehicle policy is excluded. This prevents overlap and ensures that nuclear liabilities are managed through specialized contracts rather than general vehicle insurance [Data: Entities (88, 89, 43, 44, 40); Relationships (118, 120, 250, 67, 68, +more)]. These exclusions reflect the high-risk nature of such activities and the need for specialized risk management. The policy’s approach ensures that general vehicle insurance remains focused on typical driving risks, while high-consequence events are addressed through appropriate, dedicated coverage mechanisms.

## Workers’ compensation and other insurance take precedence over policy coverage

The policy includes a hierarchy of coverage, where workers’ compensation benefits and other insurance policies take precedence over the current policy. If workers’ compensation benefits are available for an injury, coverage under this policy is excluded for the same injury. Similarly, if another insurance policy or towing protection is in place, the current policy acts as excess coverage, meaning it only applies after other collectible insurance has been exhausted [Data: Entities (86, 230); Relationships (116, 322, +more)]. This provision prevents duplication of benefits and ensures that the primary insurer is responsible for initial claims. It also aligns with broader insurance principles of coordination of benefits and risk allocation. For policyholders, this means that in cases involving workplace injuries or existing coverage, they may not receive benefits from this policy, emphasizing the importance of understanding their full insurance landscape.

## Mechanical breakdowns are excluded from coverage under the policy

Mechanical breakdown or failure—defined as the failure of mechanical, electrical, or electronic components due to normal wear or malfunction—is explicitly excluded from coverage under the policy. This exclusion applies regardless of whether the failure occurs during a ride-sharing activity or personal use. The exclusion is linked to the EXCLUSIONS category and is consistent with the policy’s focus on excluding routine vehicle maintenance issues from coverage [Data: Entities (176); Relationships (257, +more)]. This means that repairs resulting from wear and tear, such as engine failure or transmission issues, are not covered under the policy, even if the vehicle is disabled and requires towing. Policyholders must therefore rely on separate maintenance plans or warranties for such issues, reinforcing the policy’s scope as a risk management tool for accidents and emergencies rather than routine vehicle upkeep.

## The policyholder’s role in accessing roadside assistance is clearly defined

The POLICYHOLDER is the individual or entity entitled to benefits under the policy and plays a central role in accessing roadside assistance. During a covered emergency, the policyholder may receive services from an AUTHORIZED SERVICE REPRESENTATIVE, who is contracted by the insurer to deliver support such as towing, on-site labor, and lockout assistance. The policyholder is responsible for ensuring that the vehicle is towed to the nearest qualified repair facility to maintain coverage, and must use authorized providers to avoid out-of-pocket expenses [Data: Entities (214, 221); Relationships (310, 317, 316, +more)]. The policyholder’s actions directly impact the validity of claims, as failure to comply with procedures—such as using an unauthorized provider or failing to tow to the nearest facility—can result in denied coverage. This structure places responsibility on the policyholder to act in accordance with policy terms, ensuring that assistance is both timely and compliant."

10|Pet Injury Coverage and Auto Insurance Framework|"# Pet Injury Coverage and Auto Insurance Framework

The community centers on Pet Injury Coverage, a specialized add-on within auto insurance policies that provides financial protection for pets injured or killed in covered auto-related incidents. This coverage is contingent upon the presence of both Collision and Comprehensive Coverage, and is tied to key policy components such as Actual Cash Value, Loss Payable Clause, and the Appraisal process. Entities like lienholders, insurers, and policyholders are interconnected through defined legal and financial relationships that govern claim settlements, payments, and dispute resolution.

## Pet Injury Coverage is a conditional add-on dependent on core auto coverages

Pet Injury Coverage is not a standalone policy but rather a supplemental rider available within select auto insurance plans. It is activated only when the policyholder has purchased both Collision Coverage and Comprehensive Coverage for at least one covered vehicle. This dependency ensures that the coverage is only applicable in cases involving accidents, theft, vandalism, or other specified perils that are already protected under the primary policy. The requirement for these foundational coverages underscores the structured, tiered nature of the insurance framework in which Pet Injury Coverage operates [Data: Entities (153), Relationships (220, 223, 224, 226, 227, 228, +more)].

## Pet Injury Coverage provides a $1,000 total cap for death and injury benefits

Under Pet Injury Coverage, the total compensation available for a single loss event is capped at $1,000. This amount is shared between two components: a $1,000 death benefit for a pet that dies due to a covered incident, and up to $1,000 in reimbursement for veterinary fees related to injury. However, the death benefit is reduced by any veterinary expenses already paid, ensuring that the combined payout does not exceed the $1,000 limit. This cap reflects a balance between offering meaningful support and managing insurer risk. The coverage is only triggered when the incident is covered under the primary auto policy and the pet was inside the vehicle at the time of the loss [Data: Entities (153, 163, 164), Relationships (223, 224, 226, +more)].

## Actual Cash Value is central to determining claim payouts for vehicle losses

Actual Cash Value (ACV) is a critical metric used to determine the maximum payout under the policy in the event of a total loss of a covered auto. It is calculated by subtracting depreciation and other deductions from the replacement cost of the vehicle. This value serves as the benchmark for settlement amounts, ensuring that compensation reflects the vehicle’s market value at the time of loss. ACV is directly influenced by replacement cost and depreciation, both of which are defined and adjusted under Part IV of the policy. The calculation process is formalized and governed by specific policy terms, making ACV a foundational element in the insurance claims process [Data: Entities (157, 205, 206), Relationships (229, 289, 290, 291, +more)].

## Part IV governs the calculation and adjustment of loss payments

Part IV of the insurance policy outlines the detailed terms for payment of losses related to covered property. It establishes the methodology for determining actual cash value, including the use of replacement cost as a base and the adjustment for depreciation. Additionally, Part IV permits adjustments for betterment—increases in value due to improvements or upgrades—when repairing or replacing damaged property. It also includes a clause limiting payment when other insurance sources are available, ensuring that the insurer only pays its proportionate share. Furthermore, Part IV specifies that no payment is made for loss of use beyond 30 days and that window glass repairs are not subject to a deductible. These provisions collectively shape the financial and procedural framework for claim settlements [Data: Entities (202), Relationships (289, 290, 291, 292, 295, +more)].

## The Loss Payable Clause determines payment distribution to lienholders

The Loss Payable Clause specifies how payments for a loss to a covered auto are distributed. If a lienholder is listed on the declarations page, the insurer may make payments directly to them, especially if they have a legal interest in the vehicle. This clause ensures that the lienholder’s financial interest is protected, particularly in cases where the vehicle is financed. The clause is tied to the lienholder’s status and is activated when the vehicle is damaged or totaled. This mechanism supports the financial integrity of the lending process and aligns with standard insurance practices for secured vehicles [Data: Entities (208, 213), Relationships (302, 307, +more)].

## Appraisal process provides a mechanism for resolving valuation disputes

When the insurer and policyholder cannot agree on the amount of a loss, the Appraisal process is invoked. Each party appoints an appraiser to assess the value of the loss, and if the appraisers disagree, a neutral umpire is selected to resolve the dispute. If the appraisers fail to agree on an umpire within 15 days, a judge may be requested to appoint one. This structured dispute resolution mechanism ensures fairness and transparency in claim settlements, particularly in high-value or contested cases. The process is formalized and governed by policy terms, reflecting a commitment to equitable outcomes [Data: Entities (209, 216, 217, 218), Relationships (303, 304, 305, +more)].

## Covered Losses include collision, theft, vandalism, and animal strikes

A covered loss under the policy includes a range of incidents such as collisions with other vehicles or objects, theft, vandalism, natural disasters, and animal strikes. These perils are protected under either Collision Coverage or Comprehensive Coverage, both of which are prerequisites for Pet Injury Coverage to apply. The definition of a covered loss is critical because it determines whether a claim is eligible for payment. For example, a pet injured during a collision or stolen vehicle incident would qualify, but a pet injured due to illness or natural causes would not. This specificity ensures that coverage is limited to events that are both foreseeable and insurable [Data: Entities (155, 154, 165), Relationships (220, 223, 224, 226, 227, 228, +more)].

## Other Sources of Recovery clause limits insurer liability

The policy includes a provision stating that if other insurance or sources cover the same loss, the insurer will only pay its proportionate share based on its limit of liability. This clause prevents double recovery and ensures that the insurer is not responsible for the full cost of a loss when other parties are also liable. It applies across all covered losses, including those involving pet injuries or vehicle damage. This provision is part of Part IV and is designed to maintain fairness and financial responsibility among insurers and policyholders. It reflects standard industry practice in multi-layered insurance environments [Data: Entities (210), Relationships (295, +more)]."

129|CUSTOM PARTS OR EQUIPMENT|CUSTOM PARTS OR EQUIPMENT refer to specialized modifications or accessories installed on a covered auto that are not included by the manufacturer or dealership and permanently alter the vehicle’s appearance, performance, or functionality. These may include custom audio systems, performance upgrades, unique body enhancements, or other aftermarket additions. Such components are considered non-standard and are typically not covered under standard auto insurance policies unless specifically endorsed. Coverage for CUSTOM PARTS OR EQUIPMENT is subject to specific policy terms and conditions, including eligibility requirements, documentation, and coverage limits. To qualify for coverage, the modifications must be permanently affixed to the vehicle and documented with proof of purchase, installation, and value. The policy may require prior notification or endorsement to ensure the custom parts are included in the coverage. While standard policies often exclude non-factory-installed components, certain insurance plans offer optional coverage for CUSTOM PARTS OR EQUIPMENT under defined circumstances. This coverage is designed to protect the insured’s investment in personalized vehicle enhancements, ensuring that damage or loss due to covered perils—such as collision, fire, theft, or natural disasters—is compensated according to the policy’s terms. It is important to note that coverage is not automatic and must be explicitly added to the policy. The value of the custom parts is typically assessed at the time of installation and may be subject to depreciation over time. In the event of a claim, the insurer will evaluate the extent of the damage, verify the existence and condition of the custom components, and apply the policy’s limits and deductibles. Overall, CUSTOM PARTS OR EQUIPMENT are eligible for coverage under specific conditions, provided they meet the insurer’s criteria for permanence, documentation, and value. This ensures that vehicle owners who invest in personalized modifications are not left unprotected, while maintaining clear boundaries and limitations within the insurance framework.

26|COVERED AUTO|The term "COVERED AUTO" refers to a vehicle—whether owned, non-owned, or custom-equipped—that is specifically listed or otherwise insured under an auto insurance policy, as defined by the policy’s declarations page and applicable coverage terms. A covered auto is protected under the policy for liability, medical payments, and other coverages, including Comprehensive, Collision, and Uninsured/Underinsured Motorist Coverage, provided the vehicle is used in accordance with the policy’s conditions. This includes vehicles operated with permission and used in specified circumstances, such as for personal, pleasure, or business purposes, as long as they comply with the policy’s usage restrictions.

Coverage extends to vehicles that are owned by the policyholder, including additional autos, replacement autos, and trailers, whether attached or not, as long as they are explicitly included in the policy. The vehicle must also meet the policy’s requirements regarding garaging address and operator eligibility. A covered auto is subject to specific exclusions and liability limits as outlined in the policy, and its eligibility for coverage under Part I (typically Property Damage and Collision) and Part III (Uninsured/Underinsured Motorist Coverage) is contingent upon these terms.

Importantly, a covered auto is not limited to vehicles listed on the declarations page; it may also include vehicles added under policy provisions, such as those acquired after the policy’s inception or those used temporarily by the insured. The policy’s coverage applies when the vehicle is operated by an eligible driver and used in a manner consistent with the policy’s terms. This ensures that the insured vehicle, including trailers, is protected under the policy’s comprehensive and collision provisions, as well as medical payments and other applicable coverages.

In summary, a covered auto is any vehicle—owned, non-owned, or custom-equipped—that is insured under the policy, meets usage, location, and operator criteria, and is eligible for coverage under the policy’s various provisions, including liability, medical payments, comprehensive, collision, and uninsured/underinsured motorist protection. The definition encompasses a broad range of vehicles, including those listed on the declarations page, additional or replacement autos, and attached trailers, all subject to the policy’s specific terms, exclusions, and conditions.

Despite the lack of ownership, the vehicle may still be covered under the policy when operated with the permission of the rightful owner, provided specific conditions are met. This coverage typically applies when the insured uses the non-owned vehicle for personal, non-commercial purposes and the use is incidental or occasional rather than regular or primary. The coverage for a non-owned auto is generally secondary to the vehicle’s primary insurance, meaning that the policy only provides protection if the vehicle’s own insurance does not apply or is insufficient. 

The scope of coverage for a non-owned auto is determined by the policy’s terms and is typically limited to certain types of loss, such as liability for bodily injury or property damage resulting from an accident. The coverage is not automatic and is subject to the policy’s conditions, including the insured’s relationship to the vehicle and the nature of the use. Importantly, the coverage is not intended to replace the vehicle owner’s insurance but to provide a safety net in cases where the vehicle’s primary coverage is unavailable or inadequate.

In some cases, the policy may extend the broadest applicable coverage to a non-owned auto, based on the types of coverage available for other vehicles listed on the policy. This means that if the insured’s own vehicles are covered for comprehensive, collision, or other optional coverages, the non-owned auto may receive similar protection, depending on the policy language and jurisdiction. However, this broad coverage is not guaranteed and is contingent upon the specific terms of the insurance contract.

Overall, non-owned auto coverage is designed to protect the insured when they operate a vehicle they do not own, ensuring that they are not left without liability protection in the event of an accident. It is essential for policyholders to understand the limitations and conditions of this coverage, as it may not extend to all types of losses or all vehicles used. The inclusion of non-owned auto coverage in a policy is often a valuable feature for individuals who occasionally drive rental cars, borrow vehicles from friends or family, or use company vehicles for personal use, provided such use is permitted under the policy terms.

Because it is not covered under the policy, any damage, loss, or liability associated with the TRAILER must be addressed through separate insurance or risk management measures. This exclusion is consistent with standard insurance practices that treat trailers as separate entities from the towing vehicle, particularly when they are not used for commercial or passenger-related activities. Therefore, while the TRAILER may be legally operated on public roads when properly attached to a motor vehicle, it does not benefit from the protection afforded to covered autos under the policy. Users of the TRAILER are advised to obtain standalone insurance or endorsement coverage to protect against potential risks, including accidents, theft, or damage during transit. In summary, the TRAILER is a non-motorized, towed vehicle used for personal or non-commercial hauling, excluded from policy coverage regardless of its attachment to a covered auto, and requires separate risk mitigation strategies.

173|WEAR AND TEAR|WEAR AND TEAR refers to the gradual and normal deterioration of a vehicle resulting from regular use over time. This includes the natural degradation of components such as tires, brakes, suspension parts, and interior materials due to friction, exposure to environmental conditions, and routine operation. As a standard feature of vehicle operation, wear and tear is considered an expected outcome of ownership and usage, rather than a defect or damage caused by external factors. Under most vehicle insurance policies, wear and tear is explicitly excluded from coverage, meaning that repairs or replacements resulting from this natural degradation are not reimbursable by the insurer. This exclusion is consistent across policy terms and is intended to prevent coverage for routine maintenance issues that are inherent to the aging and use of a vehicle. The exclusion applies regardless of the vehicle’s make, model, or condition, and is not contingent on the presence of accidents, vandalism, or mechanical failure. Insurers classify wear and tear as a non-claimable event because it is predictable, preventable through regular maintenance, and not attributable to sudden or unforeseen incidents. As such, vehicle owners are responsible for managing and funding repairs related to wear and tear through personal maintenance budgets or service schedules. It is important to note that while wear and tear is excluded, damage caused by accidents, theft, or natural disasters may still be covered under comprehensive or collision coverage, provided the policy includes such protections. In summary, WEAR AND TEAR is a recognized and excluded condition in vehicle insurance policies, representing the inevitable decline of a vehicle’s components due to normal use, and is not eligible for insurance reimbursement.

173|WEAR AND TEAR|WEAR AND TEAR refers to the gradual and normal deterioration of a vehicle resulting from regular use over time. This includes the natural degradation of components such as tires, brakes, suspension parts, and interior materials due to friction, exposure to environmental conditions, and routine operation. As a standard feature of vehicle operation, wear and tear is considered an expected outcome of ownership and usage, rather than a defect or damage caused by external factors. Under most vehicle insurance policies, wear and tear is explicitly excluded from coverage, meaning that repairs or replacements resulting from this natural degradation are not reimbursable by the insurer. This exclusion is consistent across policy terms and is intended to prevent coverage for routine maintenance issues that are inherent to the aging and use of a vehicle. The exclusion applies regardless of the vehicle’s make, model, or condition, and is not contingent on the presence of accidents, vandalism, or mechanical failure. Insurers classify wear and tear as a non-claimable event because it is predictable, preventable through regular maintenance, and not attributable to sudden or unforeseen incidents. As such, vehicle owners are responsible for managing and funding repairs related to wear and tear through personal maintenance budgets or service schedules. It is important to note that while wear and tear is excluded, damage caused by accidents, theft, or natural disasters may still be covered under comprehensive or collision coverage, provided the policy includes such protections. In summary, WEAR AND TEAR is a recognized and excluded condition in vehicle insurance policies, representing the inevitable decline of a vehicle’s components due to normal use, and is not eligible for insurance reimbursement.

173|WEAR AND TEAR|WEAR AND TEAR refers to the gradual and normal deterioration of a vehicle resulting from regular use over time. This includes the natural degradation of components such as tires, brakes, suspension parts, and interior materials due to friction, exposure to environmental conditions, and routine operation. As a standard feature of vehicle operation, wear and tear is considered an expected outcome of ownership and usage, rather than a defect or damage caused by external factors. Under most vehicle insurance policies, wear and tear is explicitly excluded from coverage, meaning that repairs or replacements resulting from this natural degradation are not reimbursable by the insurer. This exclusion is consistent across policy terms and is intended to prevent coverage for routine maintenance issues that are inherent to the aging and use of a vehicle. The exclusion applies regardless of the vehicle’s make, model, or condition, and is not contingent on the presence of accidents, vandalism, or mechanical failure. Insurers classify wear and tear as a non-claimable event because it is predictable, preventable through regular maintenance, and not attributable to sudden or unforeseen incidents. As such, vehicle owners are responsible for managing and funding repairs related to wear and tear through personal maintenance budgets or service schedules. It is important to note that while wear and tear is excluded, damage caused by accidents, theft, or natural disasters may still be covered under comprehensive or collision coverage, provided the policy includes such protections. In summary, WEAR AND TEAR is a recognized and excluded condition in vehicle insurance policies, representing the inevitable decline of a vehicle’s components due to normal use, and is not eligible for insurance reimbursement.

If an insured person recovers from another without our written consent, and such recovery prejudices our right to recover payment, the insured person's right to payment under any affected coverage will no longer exist.

If we elect to exercise our rights of recovery against another, we will also attempt to recover any deductible incurred by an insured person under this policy unless we are specifically instructed by that person not to pursue the deductible. We have no obligation to pursue recovery against another for any loss not covered by this policy .

We reserve  the  right  to  compromise  or  settle  the  deductible  and  property  damage claims against the responsible parties for less than the full amount. We also reserve the right to incur reasonable expenses and attorney fees in pursuit of the recovery .

## JOINT AND INDIVIDUAL INTERESTS

If there is more than one named insured on this policy , any named insured may cancel or change this policy. The action of one named insured will be binding on all persons provided coverage under this policy.

## BANKRUPTCY

The bankruptcy or insolvency of an insured person will not relieve us of any obligations under this policy .

Under most vehicle insurance policies, wear and tear is explicitly excluded from coverage, meaning that repairs or replacements resulting from this natural degradation are not reimbursable by the insurer. This exclusion is consistent across policy terms and is intended to prevent coverage for routine maintenance issues that are inherent to the aging and use of a vehicle. As such, vehicle owners are responsible for managing and funding repairs related to wear and tear through personal maintenance budgets or service schedules. It is important to note that while wear and tear is excluded, damage caused by accidents, theft, or natural disasters may still be covered under comprehensive or collision coverage, provided the policy includes such protections. Under most vehicle insurance policies, wear and tear is explicitly excluded from coverage, meaning that repairs or replacements resulting from this natural degradation are not reimbursable by the insurer. We may, at our option:

- 1 . pay for the loss in money; or

We may settle any loss with you or the owner or lienholder of the property .

Coverage under this Part IV will not directly or indirectly benefit any carrier or other bailee for hire.

Payment under this Part IV for a loss to a covered auto will be made according to your interest and the interest of any lienholder shown on the declarations page or designated by you .  At our option, payment may be made to both jointly, or to either separately. However, if the covered auto is not a total loss, we may make payment to you and the repairer of the auto .

The lienholder's interest will not be protected:

- 1 . where fraud, misrepresentation, material omission, or intentional damage resulting in a denial of coverage by us has been committed by or at the direction of you or any person seeking coverage; or
2. where the loss is otherwise not covered under the terms of this policy .

If this policy is cancelled, nonrenewed or voided, the interest of any lienholder under this agreement will also terminate.

## OTHER SOURCES OF RECOVERY

If other sources of recovery also cover the loss, we will pay only our share of the loss. Our share is the proportion that our limit of liability bears to the total of all applicable

limits. However, any insurance we provide for a non-owned auto , or trailer not shown on the declarations page , will be excess over any other collectible source of recovery including, but not limited to:

- 1 . any coverage provided by the owner of the non-owned auto or trailer ;
2. any other applicable physical damage insurance; and
3. any other source of recovery applicable to the loss.

## APPRAISAL

If we cannot agree with you on the amount of a loss, then we or you may demand an appraisal of the loss. Within 30 days of any demand for an appraisal, each party shall appoint a competent appraiser and shall notify the other party of that appraiser's identity . The appraisers will determine the amount of loss. If they fail to agree, the disagreement will be submitted to a qualified umpire chosen by the appraisers. If the two appraisers are unable to agree upon an umpire within 15 days, we or you may request that a judge of a court of record, in the county where you reside, select an umpire. The appraisers and umpire will determine the amount of loss. The amount of loss agreed to by both appraisers, or by one appraiser and the umpire, will be binding. You will pay your appraiser's fees and expenses. We will pay our appraiser's fees and expenses. All other expenses of the appraisal, including payment of the umpire if one is selected, will be shared equally between us and you .   Neither we nor you waive any rights under this policy by agreeing to an appraisal.

173|WEAR AND TEAR|WEAR AND TEAR refers to the gradual and normal deterioration of a vehicle resulting from regular use over time. This includes the natural degradation of components such as tires, brakes, suspension parts, and interior materials due to friction, exposure to environmental conditions, and routine operation. As a standard feature of vehicle operation, wear and tear is considered an expected outcome of ownership and usage, rather than a defect or damage caused by external factors. Under most vehicle insurance policies, wear and tear is explicitly excluded from coverage, meaning that repairs or replacements resulting from this natural degradation are not reimbursable by the insurer. This exclusion is consistent across policy terms and is intended to prevent coverage for routine maintenance issues that are inherent to the aging and use of a vehicle. The exclusion applies regardless of the vehicle’s make, model, or condition, and is not contingent on the presence of accidents, vandalism, or mechanical failure. Insurers classify wear and tear as a non-claimable event because it is predictable, preventable through regular maintenance, and not attributable to sudden or unforeseen incidents. As such, vehicle owners are responsible for managing and funding repairs related to wear and tear through personal maintenance budgets or service schedules. It is important to note that while wear and tear is excluded, damage caused by accidents, theft, or natural disasters may still be covered under comprehensive or collision coverage, provided the policy includes such protections. In summary, WEAR AND TEAR is a recognized and excluded condition in vehicle insurance policies, representing the inevitable decline of a vehicle’s components due to normal use, and is not eligible for insurance reimbursement.

- 1 . covered auto , including an attached trailer ; or
2. non-owned auto ;

and its custom parts or equipment , resulting from collision .

In addition, we will pay the reasonable cost to replace any child safety seat damaged in an accident to which this coverage applies.

## INSURING AGREEMENT-COMPREHENSIVE COVERAGE

If you pay the premium for this coverage, we will pay for sudden, direct and accidental loss to a:

- 1 . covered auto , including an attached trailer ; or
2. non-owned auto ;

and its custom parts or equipment , that is not caused by collision .

## A loss not caused by collision includes:

- 1 . contact with an animal (including a bird);
2. explosion or earthquake;
3. fire;
4. malicious mischief or vandalism;
5. missiles or falling objects;
6. riot or civil commotion;
- 7 . theft or larceny;
8. windstorm, hail, water or flood; or
9. breakage of glass not caused by collision .

## In addition, we will pay for:

- 1 . reasonable transportation expenses incurred by you if a covered auto is stolen; and
2. loss of use damages that you are legally liable to pay if a non-owned auto is stolen. A combined maximum of $900, not exceeding $30 per day, will apply to these additional benefits. Coverage for transportation expenses and loss of use damages begins 48 hours after you report the theft to us and ends the earliest of:

2. when the auto has been recovered and repaired;
3. when the auto has been replaced;
4. 72 hours after we make an offer to settle the loss if the auto is deemed by us to be a total loss; or

5. if the loss is theft of a rented non-owned auto , 30 days after loss of use begins on the loss.

We must receive written proof of transportation expenses and loss of use damages.

We will pay for sudden, direct and accidental loss to custom parts or equipment on a covered auto for which this coverage has been purchased. This coverage applies in addition to any coverage automatically provided for custom parts or equipment under Comprehensive Coverage or Collision Coverage.

10|Pet Injury Coverage and Auto Insurance Framework|"# Pet Injury Coverage and Auto Insurance Framework

The community centers on Pet Injury Coverage, a specialized add-on within auto insurance policies that provides financial protection for pets injured or killed in covered auto-related incidents. This coverage is contingent upon the presence of both Collision and Comprehensive Coverage, and is tied to key policy components such as Actual Cash Value, Loss Payable Clause, and the Appraisal process. Entities like lienholders, insurers, and policyholders are interconnected through defined legal and financial relationships that govern claim settlements, payments, and dispute resolution.

## Pet Injury Coverage is a conditional add-on dependent on core auto coverages

Pet Injury Coverage is not a standalone policy but rather a supplemental rider available within select auto insurance plans. It is activated only when the policyholder has purchased both Collision Coverage and Comprehensive Coverage for at least one covered vehicle. This dependency ensures that the coverage is only applicable in cases involving accidents, theft, vandalism, or other specified perils that are already protected under the primary policy. The requirement for these foundational coverages underscores the structured, tiered nature of the insurance framework in which Pet Injury Coverage operates [Data: Entities (153), Relationships (220, 223, 224, 226, 227, 228, +more)].

## Pet Injury Coverage provides a $1,000 total cap for death and injury benefits

Under Pet Injury Coverage, the total compensation available for a single loss event is capped at $1,000. This amount is shared between two components: a $1,000 death benefit for a pet that dies due to a covered incident, and up to $1,000 in reimbursement for veterinary fees related to injury. However, the death benefit is reduced by any veterinary expenses already paid, ensuring that the combined payout does not exceed the $1,000 limit. This cap reflects a balance between offering meaningful support and managing insurer risk. The coverage is only triggered when the incident is covered under the primary auto policy and the pet was inside the vehicle at the time of the loss [Data: Entities (153, 163, 164), Relationships (223, 224, 226, +more)].

## Actual Cash Value is central to determining claim payouts for vehicle losses

Actual Cash Value (ACV) is a critical metric used to determine the maximum payout under the policy in the event of a total loss of a covered auto. It is calculated by subtracting depreciation and other deductions from the replacement cost of the vehicle. This value serves as the benchmark for settlement amounts, ensuring that compensation reflects the vehicle’s market value at the time of loss. ACV is directly influenced by replacement cost and depreciation, both of which are defined and adjusted under Part IV of the policy. The calculation process is formalized and governed by specific policy terms, making ACV a foundational element in the insurance claims process [Data: Entities (157, 205, 206), Relationships (229, 289, 290, 291, +more)].

## Part IV governs the calculation and adjustment of loss payments

Part IV of the insurance policy outlines the detailed terms for payment of losses related to covered property. It establishes the methodology for determining actual cash value, including the use of replacement cost as a base and the adjustment for depreciation. Additionally, Part IV permits adjustments for betterment—increases in value due to improvements or upgrades—when repairing or replacing damaged property. It also includes a clause limiting payment when other insurance sources are available, ensuring that the insurer only pays its proportionate share. Furthermore, Part IV specifies that no payment is made for loss of use beyond 30 days and that window glass repairs are not subject to a deductible. These provisions collectively shape the financial and procedural framework for claim settlements [Data: Entities (202), Relationships (289, 290, 291, 292, 295, +more)].

## The Loss Payable Clause determines payment distribution to lienholders

The Loss Payable Clause specifies how payments for a loss to a covered auto are distributed. If a lienholder is listed on the declarations page, the insurer may make payments directly to them, especially if they have a legal interest in the vehicle. This clause ensures that the lienholder’s financial interest is protected, particularly in cases where the vehicle is financed. The clause is tied to the lienholder’s status and is activated when the vehicle is damaged or totaled. This mechanism supports the financial integrity of the lending process and aligns with standard insurance practices for secured vehicles [Data: Entities (208, 213), Relationships (302, 307, +more)].

## Appraisal process provides a mechanism for resolving valuation disputes

When the insurer and policyholder cannot agree on the amount of a loss, the Appraisal process is invoked. Each party appoints an appraiser to assess the value of the loss, and if the appraisers disagree, a neutral umpire is selected to resolve the dispute. If the appraisers fail to agree on an umpire within 15 days, a judge may be requested to appoint one. This structured dispute resolution mechanism ensures fairness and transparency in claim settlements, particularly in high-value or contested cases. The process is formalized and governed by policy terms, reflecting a commitment to equitable outcomes [Data: Entities (209, 216, 217, 218), Relationships (303, 304, 305, +more)].

## Covered Losses include collision, theft, vandalism, and animal strikes

A covered loss under the policy includes a range of incidents such as collisions with other vehicles or objects, theft, vandalism, natural disasters, and animal strikes. These perils are protected under either Collision Coverage or Comprehensive Coverage, both of which are prerequisites for Pet Injury Coverage to apply. The definition of a covered loss is critical because it determines whether a claim is eligible for payment. For example, a pet injured during a collision or stolen vehicle incident would qualify, but a pet injured due to illness or natural causes would not. This specificity ensures that coverage is limited to events that are both foreseeable and insurable [Data: Entities (155, 154, 165), Relationships (220, 223, 224, 226, 227, 228, +more)].

## Other Sources of Recovery clause limits insurer liability

The policy includes a provision stating that if other insurance or sources cover the same loss, the insurer will only pay its proportionate share based on its limit of liability. This clause prevents double recovery and ensures that the insurer is not responsible for the full cost of a loss when other parties are also liable. It applies across all covered losses, including those involving pet injuries or vehicle damage. This provision is part of Part IV and is designed to maintain fairness and financial responsibility among insurers and policyholders. It reflects standard industry practice in multi-layered insurance environments [Data: Entities (210), Relationships (295, +more)]."

This includes the natural degradation of components such as tires, brakes, suspension parts, and interior materials due to friction, exposure to environmental conditions, and routine operation. As a standard feature of vehicle operation, wear and tear is considered an expected outcome of ownership and usage, rather than a defect or damage caused by external factors. Under most vehicle insurance policies, wear and tear is explicitly excluded from coverage, meaning that repairs or replacements resulting from this natural degradation are not reimbursable by the insurer. This exclusion is consistent across policy terms and is intended to prevent coverage for routine maintenance issues that are inherent to the aging and use of a vehicle. The exclusion applies regardless of the vehicle’s make, model, or condition, and is not contingent on the presence of accidents, vandalism, or mechanical failure. Insurers classify wear and tear as a non-claimable event because it is predictable, preventable through regular maintenance, and not attributable to sudden or unforeseen incidents. As such, vehicle owners are responsible for managing and funding repairs related to wear and tear through personal maintenance budgets or service schedules. It is important to note that while wear and tear is excluded, damage caused by accidents, theft, or natural disasters may still be covered under comprehensive or collision coverage, provided the policy includes such protections. The policy does not provide financial protection for such incidents, meaning that any costs associated with repairs, replacements, or mitigation efforts stemming directly from freezing conditions must be borne by the policyholder. This exclusion is a standard provision in many insurance policies, particularly in property and homeowners insurance, to manage risk associated with natural phenomena that are often preventable through proper maintenance and preparation. While the policy may cover other types of damage—such as fire, theft, or windstorm—the specific risk of freezing is not included, regardless of whether the damage occurred due to sudden freezing events or prolonged exposure to cold temperatures. It is important for policyholders to understand that even if they have taken preventive measures, such as insulating pipes or maintaining indoor heating, the policy will not compensate for losses caused by freezing if those measures fail. The exclusion remains in effect unless specifically endorsed or modified through a supplemental policy or rider. Therefore, individuals in regions prone to freezing weather are advised to consider additional coverage or proactive risk management strategies to protect against potential losses. In summary, "FREEZING" denotes a category of damage caused by low temperatures that is consistently excluded from the policy’s scope of coverage, emphasizing the need for policyholders to be aware of this limitation and to take independent steps to mitigate freezing-related risks.

263|RECOVERY RIGHTS|RECOVERY RIGHTS refer to the legal entitlements of an insurance company to seek reimbursement from a third party or, in certain circumstances, from the insured person after the insurer has made a payment under a policy. This right arises when the insurer has compensated the insured for a loss that was caused by a liable third party. In such cases, the insurer may pursue the responsible party to recover the amount paid out, including both the claim amount and any deductible the insured was required to pay. This mechanism ensures that the financial burden of the loss is ultimately borne by the party at fault, rather than the insurer or the insured. The scope of recovery rights may vary depending on the type of insurance policy, jurisdiction, and specific contractual terms. While the primary focus is on recovering funds from third parties who are legally responsible for the loss, in some instances—particularly in liability or personal injury cases—insurers may also have the right to seek reimbursement from the insured, especially if the insured was found to be partially or fully at fault. These rights are critical to maintaining the financial integrity of insurance systems by preventing unjust enrichment and promoting accountability. The exercise of recovery rights is typically governed by statutory law, policy language, and established legal precedents, and may involve legal proceedings if the liable party refuses to settle. 389|INSURED PERSON|LIABLE PARTY|The insured person, who has obtained insurance coverage for potential losses, may seek recovery of payments made by the insurer from the liable party—the individual or entity legally responsible for the loss or damage. This right to recovery arises when the insured person has been compensated by the insurer under the terms of the policy and subsequently identifies a third party (the liable party) whose actions or negligence caused the loss. The insured person’s ability to recover from the liable party is a critical component of the insurance framework, as it allows for the restoration of financial resources that were initially advanced by the insurer.

However, the recovery by the insured person from the liable party may impact the insurer’s right to reimbursement. Specifically, if the insured person successfully recovers funds from the liable party, the amount recovered may be subject to the insurer’s right to be reimbursed for the payments it made on behalf of the insured. This is typically governed by subrogation rights, which allow the insurer to step into the shoes of the insured and pursue recovery from the liable party. The extent to which the insurer can recover depends on the terms of the insurance policy and applicable legal principles.

In cases where the insured person recovers more than the insurer’s total payment, the excess may be retained by the insured, while the insurer is entitled to reimbursement up to the amount it paid. If the recovery is less than the insurer’s payment, the insurer may still be entitled to the full amount recovered, with the insured person bearing the remaining loss. The interplay between the insured person’s right to recover and the insurer’s right to reimbursement ensures that neither party is unjustly enriched, while also maintaining the integrity of the insurance system.

Ultimately, the relationship between the insured person and the liable party is governed by both contractual obligations and legal principles, with the insurer’s subrogation rights serving as a mechanism to prevent double recovery and to ensure that the party at fault bears the financial responsibility. The insured person must act in good faith and cooperate with the insurer in pursuing recovery from the liable party, as failure to do so may jeopardize the insurer’s ability to recover and could potentially affect the insured person’s future coverage or claims. The coordinated effort between the insured person and the insurer ensures a balanced and equitable resolution of claims involving third-party liability.|6

This coverage is contingent upon the presence of both Collision and Comprehensive Coverage, and is tied to key policy components such as Actual Cash Value, Loss Payable Clause, and the Appraisal process. Entities like lienholders, insurers, and policyholders are interconnected through defined legal and financial relationships that govern claim settlements, payments, and dispute resolution.

## Pet Injury Coverage is a conditional add-on dependent on core auto coverages

Pet Injury Coverage is not a standalone policy but rather a supplemental rider available within select auto insurance plans. It is activated only when the policyholder has purchased both Collision Coverage and Comprehensive Coverage for at least one covered vehicle. This dependency ensures that the coverage is only applicable in cases involving accidents, theft, vandalism, or other specified perils that are already protected under the primary policy. The requirement for these foundational coverages underscores the structured, tiered nature of the insurance framework in which Pet Injury Coverage operates [Data: Entities (153), Relationships (220, 223, 224, 226, 227, 228, +more)].

## Pet Injury Coverage provides a $1,000 total cap for death and injury benefits

Under Pet Injury Coverage, the total compensation available for a single loss event is capped at $1,000. This amount is shared between two components: a $1,000 death benefit for a pet that dies due to a covered incident, and up to $1,000 in reimbursement for veterinary fees related to injury. However, the death benefit is reduced by any veterinary expenses already paid, ensuring that the combined payout does not exceed the $1,000 limit. This cap reflects a balance between offering meaningful support and managing insurer risk. The coverage is only triggered when the incident is covered under the primary auto policy and the pet was inside the vehicle at the time of the loss [Data: Entities (153, 163, 164), Relationships (223, 224, 226, +more)].

## Actual Cash Value is central to determining claim payouts for vehicle losses

Actual Cash Value (ACV) is a critical metric used to determine the maximum payout under the policy in the event of a total loss of a covered auto. It is calculated by subtracting depreciation and other deductions from the replacement cost of the vehicle. This value serves as the benchmark for settlement amounts, ensuring that compensation reflects the vehicle’s market value at the time of loss. ACV is directly influenced by replacement cost and depreciation, both of which are defined and adjusted under Part IV of the policy. The calculation process is formalized and governed by specific policy terms, making ACV a foundational element in the insurance claims process [Data: Entities (157, 205, 206), Relationships (229, 289, 290, 291, +more)].

## Part IV governs the calculation and adjustment of loss payments

Part IV of the insurance policy outlines the detailed terms for payment of losses related to covered property. It establishes the methodology for determining actual cash value, including the use of replacement cost as a base and the adjustment for depreciation. Additionally, Part IV permits adjustments for betterment—increases in value due to improvements or upgrades—when repairing or replacing damaged property. It also includes a clause limiting payment when other insurance sources are available, ensuring that the insurer only pays its proportionate share. Furthermore, Part IV specifies that no payment is made for loss of use beyond 30 days and that window glass repairs are not subject to a deductible. These provisions collectively shape the financial and procedural framework for claim settlements [Data: Entities (202), Relationships (289, 290, 291, 292, 295, +more)].

## The Loss Payable Clause determines payment distribution to lienholders

The Loss Payable Clause specifies how payments for a loss to a covered auto are distributed. If a lienholder is listed on the declarations page, the insurer may make payments directly to them, especially if they have a legal interest in the vehicle. This clause ensures that the lienholder’s financial interest is protected, particularly in cases where the vehicle is financed. The clause is tied to the lienholder’s status and is activated when the vehicle is damaged or totaled. This mechanism supports the financial integrity of the lending process and aligns with standard insurance practices for secured vehicles [Data: Entities (208, 213), Relationships (302, 307, +more)].

## Appraisal process provides a mechanism for resolving valuation disputes

When the insurer and policyholder cannot agree on the amount of a loss, the Appraisal process is invoked. Each party appoints an appraiser to assess the value of the loss, and if the appraisers disagree, a neutral umpire is selected to resolve the dispute. If the appraisers fail to agree on an umpire within 15 days, a judge may be requested to appoint one. This structured dispute resolution mechanism ensures fairness and transparency in claim settlements, particularly in high-value or contested cases. The process is formalized and governed by policy terms, reflecting a commitment to equitable outcomes [Data: Entities (209, 216, 217, 218), Relationships (303, 304, 305, +more)].

## Covered Losses include collision, theft, vandalism, and animal strikes

A covered loss under the policy includes a range of incidents such as collisions with other vehicles or objects, theft, vandalism, natural disasters, and animal strikes. These perils are protected under either Collision Coverage or Comprehensive Coverage, both of which are prerequisites for Pet Injury Coverage to apply. The definition of a covered loss is critical because it determines whether a claim is eligible for payment. For example, a pet injured during a collision or stolen vehicle incident would qualify, but a pet injured due to illness or natural causes would not. This specificity ensures that coverage is limited to events that are both foreseeable and insurable [Data: Entities (155, 154, 165), Relationships (220, 223, 224, 226, 227, 228, +more)].

## Other Sources of Recovery clause limits insurer liability

The policy includes a provision stating that if other insurance or sources cover the same loss, the insurer will only pay its proportionate share based on its limit of liability. This clause prevents double recovery and ensures that the insurer is not responsible for the full cost of a loss when other parties are also liable. It applies across all covered losses, including those involving pet injuries or vehicle damage. This provision is part of Part IV and is designed to maintain fairness and financial responsibility among insurers and policyholders. It reflects standard industry practice in multi-layered insurance environments [Data: Entities (210), Relationships (295, +more)]."

10|Pet Injury Coverage and Auto Insurance Framework|"# Pet Injury Coverage and Auto Insurance Framework

The community centers on Pet Injury Coverage, a specialized add-on within auto insurance policies that provides financial protection for pets injured or killed in covered auto-related incidents. This coverage is contingent upon the presence of both Collision and Comprehensive Coverage, and is tied to key policy components such as Actual Cash Value, Loss Payable Clause, and the Appraisal process. Entities like lienholders, insurers, and policyholders are interconnected through defined legal and financial relationships that govern claim settlements, payments, and dispute resolution.

## Pet Injury Coverage is a conditional add-on dependent on core auto coverages

Pet Injury Coverage is not a standalone policy but rather a supplemental rider available within select auto insurance plans. It is activated only when the policyholder has purchased both Collision Coverage and Comprehensive Coverage for at least one covered vehicle. This dependency ensures that the coverage is only applicable in cases involving accidents, theft, vandalism, or other specified perils that are already protected under the primary policy. The requirement for these foundational coverages underscores the structured, tiered nature of the insurance framework in which Pet Injury Coverage operates [Data: Entities (153), Relationships (220, 223, 224, 226, 227, 228, +more)].

## Pet Injury Coverage provides a $1,000 total cap for death and injury benefits

Under Pet Injury Coverage, the total compensation available for a single loss event is capped at $1,000. This amount is shared between two components: a $1,000 death benefit for a pet that dies due to a covered incident, and up to $1,000 in reimbursement for veterinary fees related to injury. However, the death benefit is reduced by any veterinary expenses already paid, ensuring that the combined payout does not exceed the $1,000 limit. This cap reflects a balance between offering meaningful support and managing insurer risk. The coverage is only triggered when the incident is covered under the primary auto policy and the pet was inside the vehicle at the time of the loss [Data: Entities (153, 163, 164), Relationships (223, 224, 226, +more)].

## Actual Cash Value is central to determining claim payouts for vehicle losses

Actual Cash Value (ACV) is a critical metric used to determine the maximum payout under the policy in the event of a total loss of a covered auto. It is calculated by subtracting depreciation and other deductions from the replacement cost of the vehicle. This value serves as the benchmark for settlement amounts, ensuring that compensation reflects the vehicle’s market value at the time of loss. ACV is directly influenced by replacement cost and depreciation, both of which are defined and adjusted under Part IV of the policy. The calculation process is formalized and governed by specific policy terms, making ACV a foundational element in the insurance claims process [Data: Entities (157, 205, 206), Relationships (229, 289, 290, 291, +more)].

## Part IV governs the calculation and adjustment of loss payments

Part IV of the insurance policy outlines the detailed terms for payment of losses related to covered property. It establishes the methodology for determining actual cash value, including the use of replacement cost as a base and the adjustment for depreciation. Additionally, Part IV permits adjustments for betterment—increases in value due to improvements or upgrades—when repairing or replacing damaged property. It also includes a clause limiting payment when other insurance sources are available, ensuring that the insurer only pays its proportionate share. Furthermore, Part IV specifies that no payment is made for loss of use beyond 30 days and that window glass repairs are not subject to a deductible. These provisions collectively shape the financial and procedural framework for claim settlements [Data: Entities (202), Relationships (289, 290, 291, 292, 295, +more)].

## The Loss Payable Clause determines payment distribution to lienholders

The Loss Payable Clause specifies how payments for a loss to a covered auto are distributed. If a lienholder is listed on the declarations page, the insurer may make payments directly to them, especially if they have a legal interest in the vehicle. This clause ensures that the lienholder’s financial interest is protected, particularly in cases where the vehicle is financed. The clause is tied to the lienholder’s status and is activated when the vehicle is damaged or totaled. This mechanism supports the financial integrity of the lending process and aligns with standard insurance practices for secured vehicles [Data: Entities (208, 213), Relationships (302, 307, +more)].

## Appraisal process provides a mechanism for resolving valuation disputes

When the insurer and policyholder cannot agree on the amount of a loss, the Appraisal process is invoked. Each party appoints an appraiser to assess the value of the loss, and if the appraisers disagree, a neutral umpire is selected to resolve the dispute. If the appraisers fail to agree on an umpire within 15 days, a judge may be requested to appoint one. This structured dispute resolution mechanism ensures fairness and transparency in claim settlements, particularly in high-value or contested cases. The process is formalized and governed by policy terms, reflecting a commitment to equitable outcomes [Data: Entities (209, 216, 217, 218), Relationships (303, 304, 305, +more)].

## Covered Losses include collision, theft, vandalism, and animal strikes

A covered loss under the policy includes a range of incidents such as collisions with other vehicles or objects, theft, vandalism, natural disasters, and animal strikes. These perils are protected under either Collision Coverage or Comprehensive Coverage, both of which are prerequisites for Pet Injury Coverage to apply. The definition of a covered loss is critical because it determines whether a claim is eligible for payment. For example, a pet injured during a collision or stolen vehicle incident would qualify, but a pet injured due to illness or natural causes would not. This specificity ensures that coverage is limited to events that are both foreseeable and insurable [Data: Entities (155, 154, 165), Relationships (220, 223, 224, 226, 227, 228, +more)].

## Other Sources of Recovery clause limits insurer liability

The policy includes a provision stating that if other insurance or sources cover the same loss, the insurer will only pay its proportionate share based on its limit of liability. This clause prevents double recovery and ensures that the insurer is not responsible for the full cost of a loss when other parties are also liable. It applies across all covered losses, including those involving pet injuries or vehicle damage. This provision is part of Part IV and is designed to maintain fairness and financial responsibility among insurers and policyholders. It reflects standard industry practice in multi-layered insurance environments [Data: Entities (210), Relationships (295, +more)]."

3. We will not pay for loss of use of a rental vehicle for more than 30 days.

## PAYMENT OF LOSS

We may, at our option:

- 1 . pay for the loss in money; or
2. repair or replace the damaged or stolen property.

At our expense, we may return any recovered stolen property to you or to the address shown on the declarations page , with payment for any damage resulting from the theft. We may keep all or part of the property at the agreed or appraised value.

We may settle any loss with you or the owner or lienholder of the property .

## NO BENEFIT TO BAILEE

Coverage under this Part IV will not directly or indirectly benefit any carrier or other bailee for hire.

## LOSS PAYABLE CLAUSE

Payment under this Part IV for a loss to a covered auto will be made according to your interest and the interest of any lienholder shown on the declarations page or designated by you .  At our option, payment may be made to both jointly, or to either separately. However, if the covered auto is not a total loss, we may make payment to you and the repairer of the auto .

The lienholder's interest will not be protected:

- 1 . where fraud, misrepresentation, material omission, or intentional damage resulting in a denial of coverage by us has been committed by or at the direction of you or any person seeking coverage; or
2. where the loss is otherwise not covered under the terms of this policy .

If this policy is cancelled, nonrenewed or voided, the interest of any lienholder under this agreement will also terminate.

## OTHER SOURCES OF RECOVERY

If other sources of recovery also cover the loss, we will pay only our share of the loss. Our share is the proportion that our limit of liability bears to the total of all applicable

limits. However, any insurance we provide for a non-owned auto , or trailer not shown on the declarations page , will be excess over any other collectible source of recovery including, but not limited to:

- 1 . any coverage provided by the owner of the non-owned auto or trailer ;
2. any other applicable physical damage insurance; and
3. any other source of recovery applicable to the loss.

## APPRAISAL

If we cannot agree with you on the amount of a loss, then we or you may demand an appraisal of the loss. Within 30 days of any demand for an appraisal, each party shall appoint a competent appraiser and shall notify the other party of that appraiser's identity . The appraisers will determine the amount of loss. If they fail to agree, the disagreement will be submitted to a qualified umpire chosen by the appraisers. If the two appraisers are unable to agree upon an umpire within 15 days, we or you may request that a judge of a court of record, in the county where you reside, select an umpire. The appraisers and umpire will determine the amount of loss. The amount of loss agreed to by both appraisers, or by one appraiser and the umpire, will be binding. You will pay your appraiser's fees and expenses. We will pay our appraiser's fees and expenses. All other expenses of the appraisal, including payment of the umpire if one is selected, will be shared equally between us and you .   Neither we nor you waive any rights under this policy by agreeing to an appraisal.

## CANCELLATION

You may cancel this policy during the policy period by calling or writing us and stating the future date you wish the cancellation to be effective.

We may cancel this policy during the policy period by mailing a notice of cancellation to the named insured shown on the declarations page at the last known address appearing in our records.

If the policy is cancelled for nonpayment of premium, we will mail notice of cancellation to you at least 15 days before cancellation takes effect. In all other cases, we will mail notice of cancellation to you at least 25 days before the cancellation takes effect.

We may cancel this policy for any reason if the notice is received by the named insured within the first 59 days of the initial policy period.

After this policy is in effect for more than 59 days, or if this is a renewal or continuation policy , we may cancel only for one or more of the following reasons:

- 1 . nonpayment of premium;
2. material misrepresentation or fraud by you with respect to any material fact in the procurement, continuation, change or renewal of this policy;
3. material misrepresentation or fraud in the submission of any claim under this policy;

6. violation of the terms or conditions of this policy .

A postal service certificate of mailing to the named insured at the insured's last known address appearing in our records will be sufficient proof of notice. If this policy is cancelled, coverage will not be provided as of the effective date and time shown in the notice of cancellation. Upon cancellation, you may be entitled to a premium refund. However, our making or offering of a refund is not a condition of cancellation.

## NONRENEWAL

If neither we nor one of our affiliates offers to renew or continue this policy , we will mail notice of nonrenewal to the named insured shown on the declarations page at the last known address appearing in our records. A postal service certificate of mailing to the named insured at the insured's last known address appearing in our records will be sufficient proof of notice. Notice will be mailed more than 33 days before the end of the policy period.

## AUTOMATIC TERMINATION

If we or an affiliate offers to renew or continue this policy and you or your representative does not accept, this policy will automatically terminate at the end of the current policy period. Failure to pay the required renewal or continuation premium when due will mean that you have not accepted our offer.

If you obtain other insurance on a covered auto , any similar insurance provided by this policy will terminate as to that covered auto on the effective date of the other insurance.

If a covered auto is sold or transferred to someone other than you or a relative , any insurance provided by this policy will terminate as to that covered auto on the effective date of the sale or transfer.

## LEGAL ACTION AGAINST US

We may not be sued unless there is full compliance with all the terms of this policy .

We may not be sued for payment under Part I-Liability T o Others until the obligation of an insured person under Part I to pay is finally determined either by judgment after trial against that person or by written agreement of the insured person, the claimant, and us . No one will have any right to make us a party to a lawsuit to determine the liability of an insured person.

We are entitled to the rights of recovery that the insured person to whom payment was made has against another, to the extent of our payment. That insured person may be required to sign documents related to the recovery and must do whatever else we require to help us exercise those recovery rights, and do nothing after an accident or loss to prejudice those rights.
